newsitem.title: USA: Pakistan must prove reform commitment-US investors.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan must prove reform commitment-US investors.

text.p: Pledges of economic reform following the ouster of Pakistan Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto buoyed investor hopes on Tuesday, but U.S. portfolio managers said they will watch to see whether actions follow words.
"A lot of investors will be watching what the new government says and in which direction it goes," said Amit Bhartia, analyst at GMO Emerging Markets.
Pakistani President Farooq Leghari said the new caretaker government would launch an economic reform program "that could determine the direction for the desired change."

In a televised speech on Tuesday, Leghari said he would not promise the reforms would meet "all the requirements for a restoration of the economy and accountability" or give immediate major relief. Earlier, Leghari dismissed Bhutto on charges of corruption and misrule.

Bhartia of GMO Emerging Markets said "Everybody has been so fed up with the situation that any change will be seen as positive," He noted that Pakistan's government "does not have a lot of room to maneuver."

U.S. investors, wary of previous unfulfilled reform commitments, said Pakistan's main challenges remain the same: a military budget off limits to parliament and an agricultural sector not subject to income taxes.

"Any government that comes into power is going to have to deal with pushing forward on those difficult issues," said Ali Naqvi, fund manager at Citibank Global Asset Management. "The actual part of the budget over which the government has any flexibility is small."
Naqvi said Pakistan could emerge from its economic predicament if the intirim government can build support for reform through a consensus or national unity coalition.

"We should remain cautious and vigilant that this seemingly postive move does not turn into something more complicated," he said. He said he hoped to see signs the government was emphasizing reform rather than embarking on a "witch hunt" of political opponents.
"What Pakistan needs is a plan that is fair to the whole population," said another fund manager at a major U.S. based mutual fund.
The fund manager said a fair plan would be "one that benefits the poor, and takes some of the richer landowners into the tax-paying net."

In September, Moody's Investors Service said it may lower Pakistan's B1 foreign currency rating, citing concerns about the country's weakneing eocnomic fundamentals, higher short term debt levels and ongoing balance of payments problems.
Contacted after the Bhutto sacking, a Moody's analyst said he could not comment on the country.
U.S. analysts echoed the sentiments of London-based investors interviewed by Reuters on Tuesday that the departure of Bhutto might give renewed life to the reform process.
Pakistan stocks offer attractive market valuations, and debt instruments could strengthen as local sentiment improves, U.S. investors said.

"There is cause to believe that we will see some progress made economically," one fund manager said. "The government needs to privatize, and to privatize effectively because to bring in foreign investors they need to show some signs of stability."
